power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .19", Sentence = "No significant relationship was found (r s = .20, p = .19, 95% CI [-.10, .47]) between linking sentences' strength of causal implication and action recommendations' strength of causal implication."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 186 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified

120 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  2 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  2 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  4 installable dependencies detected.
- 1191 statistics stored from the extracted output; 7 of 12 reported tests matched (58.3%).

summary_table.live_data_statements: The search was limited to articles published in the subject areas of Business, Management and Accounting, Psychology and Social Science.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("Interrater reliability checks.R", 
"PsyCap_Causal Inference_Analyses.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—"), Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Interrater reliability checks.R", "PsyCap_Causal Inference_Analyses.R"
), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("", ""), "Time (s)" = c(1.2, 
2.4)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```

text.text: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology.
text.formatted: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al. (2022)</ref> in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology.

text.text: Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action.
This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.'s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology.

Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles.

The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections).
This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%).
No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations.
These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations.
Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

Correlation does not imply causation: this maxim is emphasised throughout undergraduate psychology lectures and laboratories alike, warning budding researchers against drawing unwarranted causal conclusions based on observational evidence.
For causality to be determined, we need to have ruled out alternative explanations.
Randomised experiments are widely considered to be the gold standard for estimating causal effects (Rohrer, 2018).
text.formatted: Randomised experiments are widely considered to be the gold standard for estimating causal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rohrer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: They allow us to establish temporal direction and manipulate independent variables while controlling for confounding variables and approximating counterfactuals through control groups, allowing researchers to identify causal relationships.

RCTs are not infalliblefoot_0 , but their key benefit is their capacity to rule out wide sets of alternative explanations for an apparent relationship between an independent variable (IV) and a dependent variable (DV).
text.formatted: RCTs are not infallible<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> , but their key benefit is their capacity to rule out wide sets of alternative explanations for an apparent relationship between an independent variable (IV) and a dependent variable (DV).

text.text: By manipulating the IV, RCTs can rule out the possibility that an apparent relationship is due to the DV affecting the IV.

By using random assignment of units to conditions, RCTs can also prevent variables that affect both the IV and the DV (whether observed or unobserved) from biasing the estimate of the causal effect -although such variables can still produce random error in the estimate.
Causal language such as 'increase' and 'improve' conveys causal relationships in which one variable is put forward as influencing another (Adams et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Causal language such as 'increase' and 'improve' conveys causal relationships in which one variable is put forward as influencing another <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Of course, not all research on human behaviour is experimental.
Researchers often seek simply to describe or predict human behaviour, and such goals can be pursued without experimentation.
In other contexts, researchers do wish to answer questions about causal effects, yet cannot conduct experiments due to ethical issues or feasibility.
In both cases, PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS researchers may end up conducting observational studies.
In observational studies, researchers typically avoid explicit causal inferences (Alvarez-Vargas et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In observational studies, researchers typically avoid explicit causal inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alvarez-Vargas et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Yet elements of their discussion -especially recommendations for action -may implicitly assume that causal effects have been demonstrated (Rohrer et al., 2021; Rohrer, 2024).
text.formatted: Yet elements of their discussion -especially recommendations for action -may implicitly assume that causal effects have been demonstrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Rohrer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Rohrer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This can lead to careless conclusions derived from intuition and unarticulated assumptions (Rohrer et al., 2021; Rohrer, 2024).

text.text: A lack of clarity can see motte-and-bailey strategies arise, where researchers make exciting but hard-to-defend causal interpretations of their findings (the bailey), then retreat to the irrefutable yet often unimportant descriptive findings (the motte) (Grosz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A lack of clarity can see motte-and-bailey strategies arise, where researchers make exciting but hard-to-defend causal interpretations of their findings (the bailey), then retreat to the irrefutable yet often unimportant descriptive findings (the motte) <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grosz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, it is not uncommon for an observational study to be published where causal language is avoided throughout the hypotheses, methods, and results section, yet the research question or analyses selected are causal in nature or the implications and recommendations given in the discussion section necessitate a causal interpretation.

If another researcher were to critique this study's approach or conclusion, the original researcher can 'retreat' to the position that their findings were descriptive -even if this is an almost trivial reading of the study.
As Grosz et al. (2020) wrote: '"The study did not correctly answer the question it did not explicitly try to answer" is not a compelling criticism' (p. 1247).
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Grosz et al. (2020)</ref> wrote: '"The study did not correctly answer the question it did not explicitly try to answer" is not a compelling criticism' (p. 1247).

text.text: When underlying assumptions about variables and causal mechanisms are not made explicit, the overstatement of findings during subsequent interpretation is more likely, and errors made in the research process are difficult to pick up (Grosz et al., 2020; Hernán, 2018).
text.formatted: When underlying assumptions about variables and causal mechanisms are not made explicit, the overstatement of findings during subsequent interpretation is more likely, and errors made in the research process are difficult to pick up <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grosz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hernán, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Observational research findings are often consistent with a number of potential theories about causal effects, which, in turn, would have different implications for decision-makers (Alvarez-Vargas et al., 2020).

text.text: Consumers of research, including researchers, practitioners, lay persons, and policymakers, may be unaware that action recommendations PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS rely on unstated assumptions, with potentially important consequences for how research is implemented.
Causal inference based on observational data is not a straightforward endeavour, but it is not impossible.
A multitude of study designs can be useful in ruling out alternative explanations.

Cross-sectional or longitudinal observational studies implementing statistical third-variable control, or more design-based approaches such as regression discontinuity designs and instrumental variable estimation are all examples of methods which can support causal inference, although no study, by itself, is sufficient to establish causality.
Through coherent causal inference frameworks, however, assumptions and implications underlying causal interpretations can be made explicit and precise (Rohrer et al., 2021; Rohrer, 2024).
text.formatted: Through coherent causal inference frameworks, however, assumptions and implications underlying causal interpretations can be made explicit and precise <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Rohrer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Rohrer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Rohrer (2018) explores how directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) can provide a principled approach to causal inference in observational research, using directed arrows to visually represent the causal assumptions underlying causal inferences.

Regardless of the study design employed, observational researchers must be transparent about their goals of causal inference, when that is in fact a goal, and about the associated assumptions underlying research decisions (Grosz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Regardless of the study design employed, observational researchers must be transparent about their goals of causal inference, when that is in fact a goal, and about the associated assumptions underlying research decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grosz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although commentaries have established the risk that implied causality in observational research poses, it is valuable to conduct systematic research into how this can manifest.
One such study by Haber et al. (2022) looked at the use of causal and associational language in observational health research.
text.formatted: One such study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al. (2022)</ref> looked at the use of causal and associational language in observational health research.

text.text: Specifically, they estimated the extent to which causality was implied by the language used to link exposures and outcomes ('linking language') and in action recommendations, and they evaluated how aligned the language and recommendations were.
Haber et al. found that although few studies explicitly stated having an interest in estimating causality, many used linking language which implied causality.

Additionally, they found that the majority of action recommendations implied causality, and PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS in 44.5% of the articles the action recommendations implied a greater level of causality than the linking sentence.

Their research demonstrated that avoiding causal language does not in itself ensure clarity of interpretation in health literature, calling for greater transparency about causal interests and reasoning.
To our knowledge, no such investigation into causal implications has been conducted in industrial-organisational (IO) psychology research.
This is important, because much research in IO psychology often takes an observational form, and (as a highly applied field) such research often contains action recommendations.
Below, we introduce psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the IO psychology and management literature which is often explored through observational research.

We use this construct as a topical vehicle to examine whether the norm of avoiding causal language and issues with subsequent implications identified in Haber et al.'s (2022) study extends to the domain of IO psychology.
text.formatted: We use this construct as a topical vehicle to examine whether the norm of avoiding causal language and issues with subsequent implications identified in <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al.'s (2022)</ref> study extends to the domain of IO psychology.

text.text: First proposed by Luthans et al. in 2004, PsyCap consists of the combined psychological resources of hope, self-efficacy, resilience, and optimism, often referred to as HERO.
text.formatted: First proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Luthans et al. in 2004</ref>, PsyCap consists of the combined psychological resources of hope, self-efficacy, resilience, and optimism, often referred to as HERO.

text.text: This growing interest is unsurprising given the increasing focus on employee wellbeing both pre-and post-pandemic (e.g.
Joly, 2020; Nielsen et al., 2017), with organisations often eager to equip their employees with personal resources to optimise their psychological wellbeing and performance in the workplace.

text.text: If PsyCap is to be applied within organisations, as has been proposed, it is critical that the causal reasoning within the literature is transparent and robust.
This study is a small-scale conceptual replication of Haber et al.'s (2022) study which evaluated how causal and associational language is used in observational health research.
text.formatted: This study is a small-scale conceptual replication of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al.'s (2022)</ref> study which evaluated how causal and associational language is used in observational health research.

text.text: Here, we apply Haber et al.'s focus to an entirely different domain of research: PsyCap.

In line with Haber et al.'s (2022) primary research questions, we aimed to: (1) identify the linking words and phrases used to describe relationships between predictors and outcomes in PsyCap literature, (2) generate estimates of the strength of causality stated or implied by the linking phrases and sentences in the PsyCap literature, (3) examine the prevalence of action claims, recommendations, and other implications that would require causal inference to have been made, and (4) examine the prevalence of misalignments between causal implications of linking language and subsequent action implications.
text.formatted: In line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al.'s (2022)</ref> primary research questions, we aimed to: (1) identify the linking words and phrases used to describe relationships between predictors and outcomes in PsyCap literature, (2) generate estimates of the strength of causality stated or implied by the linking phrases and sentences in the PsyCap literature, (3) examine the prevalence of action claims, recommendations, and other implications that would require causal inference to have been made, and (4) examine the prevalence of misalignments between causal implications of linking language and subsequent action implications.

text.text: In addition to these questions, this study pursues some secondary research aims: (1) To examine whether PsyCap studies contain a transparent acknowledgement of an intent to draw causal inferences, (2) To examine whether PsyCap studies contain explicit causal disclaimer statements, and whether causal links are implied anyway, and PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS (3) To examine whether the authors explicitly used any strategies to increase credibility of causal inferences, such as explaining the intent of controlling/adjusting for a variable.

While the present study's approach was strongly influenced by Haber et al.'s (2022) study of causal language in observational health research, some key differences exist due to the smaller scale of this study and the different domain of interest.

A sample size of 50 (plus an additional 2 for training) was selected for a margin of error of no more than 15% in estimates of proportions at the 95% confidence level.
The margin of error (MOE) for a proportion is a function of the population proportion (p) and the sample size: MOE = 1.96 sqrt(p(1-p)/n).
We assumed a 50% population proportion (p) for the sake of being conservative, since this is the value that produces the largest margin of error.

The margin of error for proportions was used as the basis for sample size determination because of the descriptive focus of this study, as several of the main analyses are centred on reporting for proportions.

To be included in the analysis, a paper had to include a research question concerned with the relationship between PsyCap and one or more other variables, in which PsyCap was a predictor variable, outcome variable or mediator.
The research questions must have been examined quantitatively using primary data, with a non-experimental research design.

Independent and Outcome Variables.
The independent and outcome variables of each article were identified.
The sentence which contained the most prominent linking phrase(s) between independent and outcome variables in both the abstract and the discussion was identified.
This sentence had to include PsyCap as one of the variables of interest.
From each linking sentence, the key linking word or phrase in reference to PsyCap was identified.
Prior to analysis, the root of each linking word was extracted.

Prior to publication, an independent rater was enlisted to conduct independent double coding with the objective of addressing the subjective nature of the causal strength ratings.
The independent rater was trained using the same method employed by the first and second author.

Specifically, the independent rater was trained by applying the review tool to four articles: the two training articles used by the first author and second author when refining the review tool, and an additional two articles new to both first author (initial rater) and the independent rater.
The first author also reviewed these additional articles.
The first author and independent rater then compared the data extracted across the four articles, using this discussion to calibrate the ratings.

For the training articles, both the first author (initial rater) and independent rater extracted data according to the full review tool, including identifying the linking sentences and action recommendations.
Applying the full review tool to the training articles was intended to help the independent rater experience the conditions of the initial rating of the articles.

For the purposes of calculating interrater reliability, when the independent rater re-rated the original 50 articles, they extracted data from the already-identified linking sentences and action recommendations.
This reflects the independent rater's role of reducing subjectivity of the casual strength ratings, as opposed to establishing consistency in sentence selection.
Other than sentence extraction, the independent rater extracted the data as per the review tool.
The articles were reviewed in the same order as the initial ratings.
The independent rater followed the review tool's protocol for root word extractions and casual implication ratings.
PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS The interrater reliability was then calculated.

Cohen's kappa was used for dichotomous or other nominal ratings to determine the agreement between the ratings beyond the level expected by chance (Cohen, 1960), and for the ordinal variables a weighted kappa was applied to account for degree of disagreement (Cohen, 1968).

This study only included data collected from public documents and therefore no ethics application or low risk notification was completed.

The root word most commonly used to link predictor and outcome in the primary linking sentence of the abstracts was "relate" (n = 13/50, 26%, 95% CI [16, 39]), followed by "influence" (n = 5/50, 10%, 95% CI [0, 23]).
Other commonly identified root words included "predict", "impact", and "affect".
The primary linking sentences of the abstracts were most commonly rated as having a strong implication, at 48% (n = 24/50, 95% CI [36, 64]) of the articles.
Thirty-six percent were rated as having no causal implication (n = 18/50, 95% CI [24, 52]), and a weak causal implication in 16% (n = 8/50, 95% CI [4, 32]).

In the discussion sections, "relate" was again the most common linking root word identified within each article's primary linking sentence (n = 17/50, 34%, 95% CI [22, 48], followed by "effect" (n = 8/50, 16%, 95% CI [4, 30]) and then "influence" (n = 7/50, 14%, 95% CI [2, 28]).

A two-tailed Spearman's rho rank correlation at a 5% alpha level was conducted to estimate the relationship between the strength of causal implication of the linking language and the strength of causality implied in the action recommendation within a given article's discussion section.
No significant relationship was found (r s = .20, p = .19, 95% CI [-.10, .47]) between linking sentences' strength of causal implication and action recommendations' strength of causal implication.
Importantly, the causality implied in the action recommendations was stronger than the causality implied in the linking sentences in 55% (95% CI [41, 70]) of the articles examined.

text.text: The vast majority of articles included in this study were cross-sectional, with 16% employing longitudinal approaches.
It should be noted that the models and strategies examined in the present study were selected as specific examples, and do not represent all possible approaches nor their effectiveness.
Additionally, whether or not these were used in a way which would support causal inference was not examined, rather, the existence of strategies which could be used in this way was identified.

Forty-two percent (95% CI [30, 57]) of the articles contained an explicit causal disclaimer statement, which was defined as any statement in the discussion which explicitly mentioned the need for caution around inferences of causality, for example "The data used in the study are mainly cross-sectional data, which cannot inform the causal relationship between variables" (Peng et al., 2022, p. 12).

text.text: Notably, 62% of the articles which explicitly warned against causal interpretations also implied some degree of causality through linking language in the abstract and 57% made action recommendations which could only be made appropriately had a causal relationship been identified.

text.text: The kappa estimates ranged from κ = .74-.96, with the exception of acknowledgement of intent to draw causal inference, for which κ = .49.
Percent agreement between raters ranged from 85% to 98%.
This study examined the causal nature and implications of language used to link variables within the observational PsyCap literature.

The majority of primary linking sentences were found to imply some level of causality, despite the fact that very few articles explicitly stated an intent to estimate causal effects and many explicitly warned against drawing causal inferences.
The majority of action recommendations had strong causal implications.
Moreover, the causal implications of the action recommendations were often stronger than the causal implications of the linking language.
In fact, no significant relationship was found between the strength of causality implied in linking sentences and action recommendations.

PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS These findings echo those of Haber et al. (2022) in the clear misalignment between the causal implications of the linking language used when reporting results and that of the subsequent action recommendations, and the use of action recommendations that implied causation in articles which gave disclaimers about inferring causation.
text.formatted: PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS These findings echo those of <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Haber et al. (2022)</ref> in the clear misalignment between the causal implications of the linking language used when reporting results and that of the subsequent action recommendations, and the use of action recommendations that implied causation in articles which gave disclaimers about inferring causation.

text.text: Many substantive research questions in psychology concern causal effects and thus discussions often hinge upon a causal interpretation (Rohrer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Many substantive research questions in psychology concern causal effects and thus discussions often hinge upon a causal interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Rohrer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It may therefore be unsurprising that some level of causality was implied in the linking statements of more than half of the abstracts and discussion sections that were examined, despite the observational nature of these studies.
In the present sample, action recommendations were most commonly rated as having strong causal implications, in that they could only be made appropriately had a causal relationship been identified.
In fact, none of the action recommendations identified were rated as having no causal implication whatsoever.
Critically, the action recommendations had stronger causal implications than the linking sentences in over half of the articles examined, with no significant relationship found between the two.
This lack of alignment could lead to decision-makers and practitioners unwittingly acting on recommendations despite the lack of an appropriate evidence base.
These findings suggest that the PsyCap literature is not immune to the motte-and-bailey strategies Grosz et al. (2020) warn of.
text.formatted: These findings suggest that the PsyCap literature is not immune to the motte-and-bailey strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Grosz et al. (2020)</ref> warn of.

text.text: The authors of the articles that were reviewed in this study were often found to give action recommendations which were exciting and impactful for organisations and employees, but which depended upon causal interpretations of their results (the bailey).
However, the descriptive nature of the results could also provide a retreat (the motte) if challenged (Grosz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, the descriptive nature of the results could also provide a retreat (the motte) if challenged <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grosz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, many articles recommended implementing PsyCap training for employees, implying that this would lead to improvements in a variable of interest, but without evidence of this causal effect.

PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS Without carefully designed causal frameworks, explicit assumptions, and methods to test causal inference (which can be critiqued by research consumers who can then decide whether or not they agree with the conclusions), a correlational study cannot determine whether, for example, PsyCap increases performance, if higher performance leads to higher PsyCap, or if some third variable affects both performance and PsyCap.
Each of these potential relationships has different implications for decision-makers.

Where recommendations imply that the temporal direction of a relationship has been established and that one variable is effecting change in another, there is an implication that this is based on evidence of causation.
It is easy to see the risk this poses.
Where inappropriate implications and recommendations are made, applications and interventions may be ineffectual or even harmful.
This is costly for organisations and their employees, and risks undermining the credibility of researchers who promote, and practitioners who apply, the research findings.

If all intentions, research decisions and assumptions about establishing causation were transparently communicated, consumers and decision-makers would be better positioned to evaluate recommendations and make informed decisions.

Almost half the articles in the study included a statement explicitly cautioning against drawing causal conclusions, despite, incongruously, many of these same articles implying some degree of causality in their linking sentences and making recommendations for action which could only be appropriate had a causal relationship been identified.

Many of these same articles implied some degree of causality in their linking sentences and gave action recommendations which could only be made appropriately had a causal relationship been identified.

This suggests that the PsyCap literature is subject to what Tennant and Murray (2021) term 'Schrödinger's inference', "where the authors caution against causal interpretations while themselves offering causal interpretations" (p.e2).
The message is clear: PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS the inclusion of disclaimers does not necessarily mean causal interpretations have been avoided.

It is evident that warning against drawing causal conclusions from observational research does not prevent causal inference within the PsyCap literature, or even the use of causal language when reporting results.
Causal intentions are often murky, emerging through the linking language used to report results and the action recommendations made.

As the research community re-evaluates the unhelpful norms and structural problems which threaten the field's credibility (e.g. Grand et al., 2018; Grosz et al., 2020; Keener et al., 2023; Vazire, 2018; Vazire et al., 2022), the way causal inference is approached needs to be reconsidered.
text.formatted: As the research community re-evaluates the unhelpful norms and structural problems which threaten the field's credibility (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Grand et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Grosz et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Keener et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Vazire, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vazire et al., 2022)</ref>, the way causal inference is approached needs to be reconsidered.

text.text: That which has previously been unstated must be made explicit and verifiable.
If the research objective is to establish causation, authors must say so and must take steps to increase the credibility of any claims made.
Researchers with causal interests should ensure they are applying the methods and research design which best support this.
All else being equal, true experimental designs can most credibly rule out alternative explanations for a hypothesised effect.
We thus encourage researchers seeking to make causal inferences about the causes or consequences of PsyCap to consider experimental studies when they are feasible.

Where observational studies are required, causal inference frameworks such as graphical causal models can be applied to support causal interpretations through intensive formalisation which requires precise questions to be asked and assumptions and their derived implications to be articulated (Rohrer & Murayama, 2023).
text.formatted: Where observational studies are required, causal inference frameworks such as graphical causal models can be applied to support causal interpretations through intensive formalisation which requires precise questions to be asked and assumptions and their derived implications to be articulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Rohrer & Murayama, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As Rohrer et al. (2021) highlights, while frameworks are no panacea, they may facilitate more productive debates.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Rohrer et al. (2021)</ref> highlights, while frameworks are no panacea, they may facilitate more productive debates.

text.text: In addition to frameworks, methodological approaches can enhance the credibility of causal inferences.

For example, longitudinal studies and natural experiments can aid in causal PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS inference in observational research (Grosz et al., 2024; Rohrer & Murayama, 2023).
text.formatted: For example, longitudinal studies and natural experiments can aid in causal PSYCHOLOGICAL CAPITAL: CAUSAL IMPLICATIONS inference in observational research <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Grosz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Rohrer & Murayama, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Ultimately, the goal should be to maximise the plausibility of causal inferences through transparent reporting of the evidence base, using the best methods available within the constraints of feasibility, informed by strong theory (Foster, 2010).
text.formatted: Ultimately, the goal should be to maximise the plausibility of causal inferences through transparent reporting of the evidence base, using the best methods available within the constraints of feasibility, informed by strong theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Foster, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As academics face intense publication pressures, it is possible that avoiding causal language yet making causally-dependent action recommendations is a reflection of conflicting incentives.

In order to be published, authors are incentivised to meet reviewers' expectations that causal language be avoided in observational research, while at the same time needing to argue that their findings offer a significant contribution to the field.

Allowing for explicit causal reasoning in carefully considered and appropriately designed observational studies could create the conditions in which authors feel able to be transparent about their intentions.
By surfacing assumptions about causality, disconnects between research findings and their interpretation will be subject to greater checks and balances.

Reviewers and publishers must be cognisant of implied causality, and rather than simply monitoring whether causal language has been used, they should question plausibility given the evidence presented and attend more closely to the consistency between claims about causal effects and action recommendations.

Practitioners and consumers of research must also recognise cases where articles make action recommendations based on causal inferences, and critically evaluate the strength of evidence for those inferences when deciding which organisational actions to take.
Descriptive findings cannot be used as the basis for recommending or implementing interventions (Grosz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Descriptive findings cannot be used as the basis for recommending or implementing interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grosz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Causal questions must be explicit and supported by the appropriate strategies, assumptions, and research decisions, to allow a critical lens to be used.

The small sample size of only 50 articles is a notable limitation that reduces the statistical power and precision of this study and may mean that only a small proportion of the PsyCap literature has been represented in the sample.
This could limit the external validity of these findings.
This reduced precision is reflected in the broad confidence intervals generated.
Another limitation is the subjective nature of the causal implication ratings.
To mitigate this limitation, an independent double coding was conducted with an independent rater in order to estimate interrater reliability.

Our findings revealed a high level of interrater reliability and agreement across the board. 2This study's scope was limited in that it did not directly evaluate the suitability of the articles' study designs or methods for supporting causal inference.
text.formatted: Our findings revealed a high level of interrater reliability and agreement across the board. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">2</ref>This study's scope was limited in that it did not directly evaluate the suitability of the articles' study designs or methods for supporting causal inference.

text.text: A thorough evaluation of study design and methodology would have provided greater insight into the extent that causal inference is employed and supported in these observational studies.
This study has only addressed causal inference within the PsyCap literature, which is a small area of IO psychology research and practice, so the findings may not be generalisable to other areas.
Nevertheless, there is a clear need for researchers and practitioners alike to remain wary of implicit causal reasoning in research articles.
It would be valuable to explore linking language and causal implications in other areas of IO psychology, to better understand the generalisability of this study's findings.
Additionally, examining the quality of causal models used in observational IO psychology research and the strength of evidence they provide would be a valuable addition to the literature.
Such research could offer important insight into whether these models are being applied in a way which would warrant causal inference.
Future studies would benefit from using a larger sample size and a larger number of raters to account for the subjective nature of causality ratings.
Additionally, it would be prudent to ensure the rater pool was made up of individuals representative of the wide range of populations which could interact with the research (Haber et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, it would be prudent to ensure the rater pool was made up of individuals representative of the wide range of populations which could interact with the research <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Haber et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This study demonstrates that the issue of unarticulated causal inference extends to PsyCap research.

Recommendations for action are regularly being made which depend upon a causal effect having been established, despite such a causal interpretation being unfounded or even explicitly cautioned against.

These findings reinforce the dangers of not surfacing causal reasoning in observational studies and demonstrate the need for more comprehensive training for students, researchers, and reviewers on the complexities of causal inference.
Causal interests and research decisions with potential causal implications must be made clear, allowing for critical consumption of research.
